explanation: The old ball measured 38 mm. The switch came after the Sydney Olympics: a bigger ball meets more air resistance, so rallies run a little slower and are easier to follow on television.

claims.text: The table tennis ball adopted for official play in 2000 has a diameter of 40 mm.
The ball adopted in 2000 is not 32 mm, 35 mm or 38 mm across.
Before the change, the official table tennis ball measured 38 mm across.
The International Table Tennis Federation brought in the 40 mm ball in October 2000, after the Sydney Olympic Games.
The larger ball was adopted to slow the game slightly and make rallies easier for spectators and television viewers to follow.

writerNotes: Subtopic: racket sports, equipment. lint: clean. claims: five, every one with a number or date marked high. datasets: no pinned dataset covers table tennis equipment; c1, c3 and c4 need web evidence (the ITTF or a reference work). I did not spend a search on it: the 38 mm to 40 mm switch in 2000 is widely documented. rivalTest: 38 mm is the planted trap (the old ball), so a player who half remembers the size picks it; 32 and 35 are spaced like the other distractors and are wrong under any reading. Argued against the key: some writers round the new ball to '40+' after the 2014 change from celluloid to plastic, but the diameter stayed 40 mm; only the material changed. The stem says 'In 2000' so the item is dated. Key sits fourth in ascending order. volatility: dated (the year is in the stem). regional: table tennis is played on every continent. style: Oxford spelling, explanation of 33 words. myths: screened, no match. mystery and encore: not applicable. doubts: the exact month (October 2000) in c4; if a checker cannot place it, c4 can drop to 'in 2000' without touching the explanation, which only says 'after the Sydney Olympics'.

evidence.restatement: Since the ITTF switch in 2000, the regulation ball for sanctioned table tennis is 40 millimetres across.

claimResults.note: The ITTF equipment rules have specified a 40 mm ball since the 2000 change; I answered 40 mm cold with high confidence. No dataset covers equipment rules; per memo 18 a direct certain confirmation by both passes carries this high-risk number.

evidence.restatement: None of 32, 35 or 38 millimetres is the size of the post-2000 ball; 38 mm was the size it replaced, and 32 and 35 were never regulation sizes in the modern era.

claimResults.note: 38 mm is the pre-2000 ball (the most tempting wrong pick); 32 and 35 mm match no standard in force after 2000. Each distractor is definitely wrong.

evidence.restatement: The ball used before the 2000 switch had a 38 millimetre diameter.

claimResults.note: The well-known '38 mm to 40 mm' change; checked against my knowledge of ITTF equipment history.

evidence.restatement: The ITTF made the larger ball mandatory in October 2000, straight after the Sydney Games, which were the last Olympics played with the 38 mm ball.

claimResults.note: The Sydney Olympics ran 15 September to 1 October 2000 and were the last major event with the 38 mm ball; the 40 mm ball took effect that October. 'October 2000, after Sydney' holds.

evidence.restatement: The ITTF chose a bigger ball so it would travel and spin a little less, giving longer, more watchable rallies for spectators and TV.

claimResults.note: The stated motive (slower play, better for television) is the ITTF's widely reported rationale; the explanation's air-resistance wording is physically sound.

evidence.restatement: Official table tennis balls have been 40 mm across since the ITTF changed the standard from the earlier smaller size in 2000.

claimResults.note: Rival test: 38 mm is the pre-2000 size and the only distractor with real pull, but the stem fixes the new ball. The 2014 plastic ball is also 40 mm, so no second answer. High-risk number: confirmed directly (memo 18). One web search on the ITTF change gave 1 October 2000 effective, but the summary cited no single result and mixed in blogs, so I do not cite it as evidence.

evidence.restatement: No official ball was ever 32 mm or 35 mm; the 2000 change went from 38 mm up to 40 mm.

claimResults.note: 38 mm is the previous size, so it is wrong for the ball adopted in 2000.

evidence.restatement: The standard ball before the ITTF's 2000 rule change was the 38 mm ball.

claimResults.note: Agrees with the search summary (38 mm to 40 mm).

evidence.restatement: The ITTF's larger ball took effect on 1 October 2000, the day the Sydney Games closed.

claimResults.note: Sydney ran 15 September to 1 October 2000, so 'after' the Games is fair. The search summary also gave 1 October 2000.

evidence.restatement: The ITTF's stated reason was that a bigger ball is slowed more by air and spins less, giving longer rallies that television viewers can follow.

claimResults.note: Widely documented rationale; the search summary agreed.

issues.note: The 2014 move to plastic 40+ balls could make a pedant ask which new ball, but the stem says 2000 and both are 40 mm, so the key holds.

stem: In 2000, table tennis adopted a new official ball. What diameter is that ball?
